ov: A comparative study of Shakespeare’s revenge tragedy and eight poems by Emily Dickinson. Both texts place the individual mind under pressure: Hamlet in a corrupt court, Dickinson’s speakers in private rooms of grief, death and doubt. The comparison asks how each text handles moral ambiguity, performance and mortality, and how reading one changes your reading of the other.
rub: Compare how texts handle context, values, form and language: drama and soliloquy against compressed lyric poetry.
Resonances and dissonances: shared interest in death, madness and conscience; differences in public stage versus private voice.
Reading creates new understanding: Hamlet’s theatricality sharpens how we hear Dickinson’s “show”; Dickinson’s economy sharpens how we hear Hamlet’s silences.
sum: Hamlet, prince of Denmark, returns to find his father dead and his mother married to his uncle Claudius, now king. The Ghost of old Hamlet tells him he was poisoned by Claudius and demands revenge. Hamlet feigns madness while he tests the Ghost’s truth by staging a play, the Mousetrap, which unsettles Claudius. Hamlet then spares Claudius at prayer, kills Polonius by mistake and is sent to England to die. Ophelia, abandoned and bereaved, goes mad and drowns. Hamlet returns, reflects on mortality in the graveyard and accepts providence. Claudius and Laertes rig a poisoned duel; Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet all die, and Fortinbras claims Denmark. Dickinson’s poems dramatise inner states in compact lyrics: a funeral in the brain (280), the madness of consensus (435), death as a courteous driver (712), and the show that is not the show (1206).
acts: The Ghost appears and tells Hamlet that Claudius murdered him. Hamlet swears revenge and plans an “antic disposition”.
Polonius spies on Hamlet and the court tries to read his madness. The players arrive and Hamlet plans the Mousetrap.
“To be, or not to be”, the nunnery scene and the Mousetrap. Claudius’s guilt is proven. Hamlet spares the praying Claudius and kills Polonius.
Hamlet is exiled. Ophelia goes mad and drowns. Laertes returns for revenge and Claudius plots a poisoned duel.
The graveyard scene, the duel and four deaths. Fortinbras restores a fragile order.
ch: Grieving scholar and reluctant avenger. A thinker more than an actor, who stages his thoughts through performance.
The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!
Politician and fratricide. His public language is smooth, but his private prayer shows guilt.
My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: / Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
Her swift remarriage fuels Hamlet’s disgust; her silence invites interpretation.
The lady doth protest too much, methinks.
Controlled by father and brother, then abandoned by Hamlet. Her madness exposes the cost of patriarchy.
O, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!
A spy and a windbag who stands for the court’s surveillance.
To thine own self be true.
A foil to Hamlet: he acts at once, and Claudius manipulates that speed.
I am justly killed with mine own treachery.
Loyal, rational witness who survives to tell Hamlet’s story.
Good night, sweet prince, / And flights of angels sing thee to thy rest.
Sets the plot in motion and raises doubt about whether it speaks truth.
cx: Hamlet was written c. 1599–1601, after the death of Shakespeare’s son Hamnet (1596) and around the time of his father’s death. Critics often link these losses to the play’s grief; this is interpretation, not proof. Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) lived largely in seclusion in Amherst, Massachusetts. Almost none of her poems were published in her lifetime, which helps explain their private, experimental voice.

Revenge tragedy (Kyd’s The Spanish Tragedy) was popular on the Elizabethan stage; Hamlet uses and questions the form. Beliefs about ghosts divided Catholic (purgatory) and Protestant (demon) thinking. Dickinson wrote in a New England shaped by Puritan and Calvinist faith, to which she responds with doubt, irony and unusual dashes and capitals.

1590s England feared a succession crisis as Elizabeth I aged without an heir, and the Earl of Essex’s rebellion (1601) heightened political anxiety. Dickinson wrote during and after the American Civil War (1861–65), a time of mass death that shapes her many poems about funerals and dying.

Shakespeare’s Denmark is hierarchical: divine right of kings, patriarchal control of women and surveillance as power. Dickinson’s world offered limited public roles for women, and she made the home and the mind her stage.
im: Imagery patterns in Hamlet: disease and rot (“something is rotten”), poison through the ear, the unweeded garden and theatre itself.
Millais, Ophelia (1851–52): the drowned heroine among flowers popularised a passive, romantic image of Ophelia that students can challenge.
Delacroix, Hamlet and Horatio in the Graveyard (1839): the skull as memento mori shapes how audiences imagine Hamlet.
Dickinson’s images are domestic: a funeral in the brain, a carriage ride with Death, a chamber that can be haunted. Her dashes and capitals set a visual rhythm on the page.
th: Neither text offers a simple moral answer: revenge corrupts the avenger; sanity is judged by a majority.
Module A Q1: complexities of moral ambiguity.
Truth hides behind performance: the court, the antic disposition, the Mousetrap; Dickinson’s “show”.
Module A: resonances in values and form.
Death is both fear and release, from soliloquy to graveyard and from funeral to courteous carriage.
Real or feigned madness blurs judgement. Dickinson turns sanity into a social verdict.
Module A: compare ideas and values.
Both texts locate moral struggle in the mind.
Module A Q2: perspective shaped by the earlier text.

q.t: {Seems|Technique: antanaclasis, repeating a word in a new sense. Effect: Hamlet throws Gertrude’s polite word back at her, exposing performed grief. Module link: launches the conversation about surface and truth that Dickinson’s “show” continues.}, madam? Nay, it is; {I know not ‘seems’|Technique: rejection of a word. Effect: Hamlet claims sincerity, ironically before he adopts disguise. Module link: contrast with Dickinson 1206.}.
q.m: Compare: Dickinson 1206, “The Show is not the Show”.

q.t: How {weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable|Technique: asyndetic list of falling adjectives. Effect: mimics exhaustion; the world loses value. Module link: the despair prefigures Dickinson’s inner collapse in 280.} / Seem to me all the uses of this world!
q.m: Compare: Dickinson 280, “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain”.

q.t: {Something is rotten|Technique: metaphor of disease. Effect: vague dread before the Ghost speaks. Module link: the body politic idea shapes moral ambiguity at the level of the state.} in the state of Denmark.
q.m: Context link: poisoned kingdom, succession fears.

q.t: The time is {out of joint|Technique: bodily metaphor of a dislocated limb. Effect: the political order is a broken body.}: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born {to set it right|Technique: infinitive of duty. Effect: revenge is burden, not choice; moral ambiguity begins.}!
q.m: Module A Q1: moral ambiguity of revenge.

q.t: Though this be madness, yet {there is method in’t|Technique: antithesis in an aside. Effect: the audience questions whether Hamlet performs or unravels. Module link: Dickinson 435 turns sanity into a social judgement.}.
q.m: Compare: Dickinson 435, “Much Madness is divinest Sense”.

q.t: {Denmark’s a prison.|Technique: blunt metaphor in a three-word declarative. Effect: the world as a space of surveillance and entrapment. Module link: Dickinson 670 internalises this prison as a haunted chamber.}
q.m: Compare: Dickinson 670, “One need not be a Chamber – to be Haunted –”.

My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: / {Words without thoughts never to heaven go.|Technique: antithesis and a closing couplet. Effect: Claudius’s language cannot reach heaven, so guilt survives eloquence. Module link: moral ambiguity within the villain.}
q.m: Complexity within the text: a guilty man who can still pray.

q.t: To be, or not to be, {that is the question|Technique: abstract infinitive and antithesis. Effect: personal crisis becomes a universal problem of existence. Module link: Dickinson 712 pictures death as a calm companion.}
q.m: Compare: Dickinson 712, “Because I could not stop for Death –”.

q.t: {Alas, poor Yorick!|Technique: apostrophe to a skull (memento mori). Effect: even the jester is dust. Module link: pairs with Dickinson’s composed personification of Death.} I knew him, Horatio.

{The readiness is all.|Technique: short declarative. Effect: calm acceptance contrasts earlier agonised soliloquies. Module link: ends the revenge dilemma with providence; compare Dickinson’s calm acceptance.}
q.m: Link: arc from doubt to acceptance.

q.t: {Assent – and you are sane –|Technique: dashes, antithesis and imperative. Effect: the dashes mimic enforced agreement, so sanity is shown as a social demand. Module link: complicates Hamlet’s “antic disposition”.} / Demur – you’re straightway dangerous –

{I felt a Funeral, in my Brain|Technique: metaphor and first-person confession. Effect: the mind becomes a place of mourning and moral judgement. Module link: moves public drama into private consciousness.},

{He kindly stopped for me –|Technique: personification of Death as a courteous driver. Effect: calm, ironic tone makes death civilised and ambiguous. Module link: compare Hamlet’s fear and Yorick’s skull.}

A.i: Both William Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Emily Dickinson’s selected poems refuse to treat morality as fixed. Shakespeare stages revenge as a duty that corrupts the avenger, while Dickinson suggests that the “sane” majority may be the real madness. Written amid Elizabethan anxiety about succession and nineteenth-century Puritan certainty, each text relocates the moral struggle into the individual conscience. Through revenge, madness and conscience, the texts invite readers to live with uncertainty.
b: Shakespeare presents revenge as a duty that is also a moral injury. When Hamlet laments that “the time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right”, the bodily metaphor of a dislocated limb frames Denmark as a broken body, while the infinitive “to set it right” makes justice a burden rather than a choice. His decisions to spare the praying Claudius and then to kill Polonius in error show how pursuing justice destroys the innocent. Claudius’s own confession, “My words fly up, my thoughts remain below”, adds complexity within the text, for the villain is capable of guilt. Hamlet is both righteous and destructive, and that ambiguity drives the conversation with Dickinson.

Dickinson extends this ambiguity to the question of who decides what is sane. Where Polonius observes, “Though this be madness, yet there is method in’t”, the antithesis in an aside leaves the audience unsure whether Hamlet performs or unravels. Dickinson’s “Assent – and you are sane – / Demur – you’re straightway dangerous” transfers this doubt to society, her dashes mimicking enforced agreement. Ophelia’s genuine madness reveals the damage of patriarchal control. In both texts, sanity becomes a moral judgement rather than a fact, complicating any simple division of right and wrong.

Finally, each text places the moral court inside the self. Hamlet vows, “The play’s the thing / Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king”, the rhyming couplet turning theatre into a moral weapon. Dickinson’s “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain” internalises judgement, the funeral metaphor making the mind a courtroom of mourners. The shift from public stage to private lyric alters the form of ambiguity: Shakespeare dramatises doubt among many voices, Dickinson compresses it into one. Moral ambiguity is thereby explored both between and within each text.
A.c: Ultimately, Shakespeare and Dickinson show that morality is contested rather than settled: justice corrupts, sanity depends on who judges, and conscience is a private, uncertain tribunal. Read together, the texts converse across centuries about the cost of certainty, leaving readers more questioning than before.
A.n: What to notice: a comparative thesis that names both texts and the key idea; each paragraph balances both texts (between) and finds complexity inside one text (within); technique, effect and context are all present; the last paragraph compares form (drama versus lyric).

B.i: Both Hamlet and Emily Dickinson’s poems show that moral questions are not simple. Shakespeare explores revenge and madness, and Dickinson explores sanity and conscience.
b: In Hamlet, revenge is difficult. Hamlet says, “The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right.” This shows that he does not want to be the avenger. He kills Polonius by mistake, which shows that revenge can hurt innocent people.

Dickinson also explores madness. In poem 435 she says, “Assent – and you are sane – / Demur – you’re straightway dangerous.” This shows that people think sane people agree with everyone. In Hamlet, Polonius says, “there is method in’t”, which shows that Hamlet’s madness may be a plan.

Both texts show the conscience. Hamlet says, “The play’s the thing / Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king”, and Dickinson says, “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain.” This shows that both texts are about what is in people’s minds.
B.c: In conclusion, Shakespeare and Dickinson both show that morality is not simple. They both explore the minds of people who struggle with right and wrong.
B.n: What to notice: relevant comparisons and quotes, but the comparison is brief and the analysis stays general (“this shows that…”). Moral ambiguity is not defined, and “between and within” is only partly met.

models.C: In Hamlet, Hamlet has to get revenge but is not sure. Dickinson writes about madness in her poems. They are both about moral ambiguity because they have difficult choices.
models.D: Hamlet is a play about revenge. Dickinson writes poems about death. They are both about hard things.

A.i: To a considerable extent, my perspective of Hamlet has shaped my reading of Dickinson, but the influence runs in both directions. Hamlet’s soliloquies, its obsession with mortality and its theatre of appearances train readers to hear Dickinson’s lyrics as dramatic voices, while Dickinson’s compression and calm in turn reveal what Hamlet’s language leaves unsaid. The earlier text therefore determines my interpretation by supplying the questions I ask of the later, and the later transforms my appreciation of the earlier.
b: Reading Hamlet first prepares me to see mortality in Dickinson as a dramatic encounter. Hamlet’s “To be, or not to be, that is the question” treats death as an unanswerable problem, and in the graveyard his apostrophe, “Alas, poor Yorick!”, makes mortality a memento mori. Against these anxieties, Dickinson’s “He kindly stopped for me –” personifies Death as a courteous driver. The contrast between Hamlet’s dread and her composed irony lets me appreciate how startling that calm is, an appreciation determined by the earlier text’s fear.

My understanding of Hamlet’s theatre of appearances also shapes my reading of Dickinson’s “The Show is not the Show”. Hamlet’s “I know not ‘seems’” and the Mousetrap, where performance exposes truth, teach me to look behind surfaces, so that Dickinson’s title reads as a statement about the gap between display and reality. At the same time, her madness poem, “Assent – and you are sane”, makes me reconsider Polonius’s “method in’t”: sanity itself may be a social performance. Dickinson’s lyric thus sharpens my sense of the earlier play’s question about who decides what is real.

Finally, Hamlet’s internal prison shapes how I hear Dickinson’s private rooms. “Denmark’s a prison” and the “conscience of the king” set the mind against the court, and Dickinson’s “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain” makes that conflict wholly interior. Without the play’s public stage, her compression would seem less bold; without her intimacy, the play’s soliloquies might seem less private. My perspective of the earlier text determines my interpretation of the later, but each limits the other, and I value both more for the conversation.
A.c: To a considerable extent, then, Hamlet determines how I read and value Dickinson: it supplies questions of mortality, performance and conscience. Yet Dickinson’s compression and irony reshape my appreciation of the play, making the textual conversation a two-way exchange.
A.n: What to notice: “to what extent” is answered directly with a nuanced judgement; the paragraphs move through three ideas with quotes from both texts in each; the response keeps returning to “perspective” and “interpretation and appreciation”.

B.i: My perspective of Hamlet has influenced how I read Dickinson’s poems. Both texts explore mortality, appearances and the mind.
b: Hamlet made me think about death in Dickinson. Hamlet says, “To be, or not to be, that is the question”, and he holds Yorick’s skull. Dickinson writes, “He kindly stopped for me –”, which shows that Death can be calm. This is different from Hamlet.
Hamlet also made me think about appearances. Hamlet says, “I know not ‘seems’”, and Dickinson writes, “The Show is not the Show.” This shows that things are not always as they seem.
The mind is important in both texts. Hamlet says, “Denmark’s a prison”, and Dickinson writes, “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain.” This shows that both texts are about thoughts.
B.c: In conclusion, my perspective of Hamlet has influenced how I understand Dickinson’s poems, because they have similar ideas about death, appearances and the mind.
B.n: What to notice: relevant links but little evaluation. “To what extent” is not weighed, the later text’s influence on the earlier is missing, and technique is rarely named.

fc: Define metatheatre and give an example.
Theatre that shows itself as theatre. Example: the Mousetrap, a staged murder exposing a real one.
What is dramatic irony in Hamlet?
The audience knows more than characters. Example: we know Claudius is guilty while Polonius misreads Hamlet.
Which Dickinson poem links to ‘method in’t’?
Laertes (acts at once) and Fortinbras (acts for a trifle).
What is a resonance and a dissonance?
A resonance is a shared idea or technique across texts; a dissonance is a clash in values, form or perspective.
